absent: Shadow interface acquisition and lifetime, trap enable and disable effects, and list register encoding.
Hypervisor priority save effects, doorbell delivery mechanism, and virtual element residency protocol.
Construction of the visible private interrupt mask and private identifier mapping.
Affinity extraction and compressed index lookup beyond table construction.
System register finalization, trap computation, timer enablement, and interrupt resource mapping steps.
Protected hypervisor VM and CPU initialization effects and handle allocation.
Counter configuration, overflow run-level protocol, and timer notification predicate.
Distributor enabled flag lifecycle and active-list insertion and removal rules.
Identifier allocation and invalidation protocol beyond per-CPU clear.
Pause flag lifecycle and request and kick delivery guarantees.

findings.text: Releasing a nested interrupt context preserves active priorities into a shadow interface, reflects a fixed small set of priority state back into virtual system state, clears in-use list entries, disables nested traps, and resets the used count on the owning CPU.

Active priority preservation derives a preemption width from a hardware type value and preserves one, two, or four registers per group, with wider widths preserving strictly more state and narrower widths preserving only low registers.
Active priority reads accept only a small selector range per group and treat any other selector as impossible, with each valid selector mapped to a distinct interface register.

Release of a directly injected interrupt context does nothing unless direct interrupts are supported and the virtual element is resident; otherwise residency is dropped with a doorbell choice reflecting wait status and, for nesting guests, nested return status.

Release of the newest interrupt interface does nothing when already nonresident to avoid losing control state on repeated release, otherwise saves priority state via hypervisor call, marks nonresident, and refreshes private priorities only while waiting.

Private priority refresh visits only guest-visible interrupts, extracts a narrow priority field from a packed per-CPU array, and publishes each value into the matching interrupt object under its own lock with correct reference handling.

Pending assessment delegates newest hardware to a dedicated private scan, reports idle when the distributor is disabled, treats a latched element flag as immediately pending, and otherwise scans the active list for an enabled non-active pending entry passing the control mask.

Control state is provided through a model-dispatched accessor normalizing distinct hardware encodings into a common enable, mask, grouping, and binary point view, with legacy emulation selecting between older and newer back ends at run time.

Newest pending assessment uses an effective mask from enable control, running active bitmap, and programmed mask; a zero mask means nothing can signal, otherwise each visible private interrupt is checked for enablement, priority passing, and physical line or software pending state.
Physical line queries require a hardware-backed interrupt and prefer a per-interrupt operation when present, falling back to asking the host controller for pending state.

Multiprocessing state is exposed through get and set controls plus power, stop, suspend, and query helpers; the set control accepts runnable, stopped, and suspended values and rejects any other value.

Stopping records stopped state and requests sleep with a kick, suspending records suspended state and requests suspension with a kick, and return to runnable is a plain state store; mutating paths serialize on a per-CPU lock while readers observe atomically.

Scheduling and introspection helpers report runnability from virtual lines, timer and performance notifications without an in-kernel controller, and distributor pending state while excluding stopped or paused CPUs; separate helpers report privileged mode and program counter.

Performance user notification compares current overflow indication against a run-level device level, where overflow reflects masked status further gated by global enables and by counters reserved for higher privilege when nesting is present.

The counter set reserved for higher privilege is empty without nesting or when the partition control is out of range, and otherwise covers a contiguous high range from the partition point to the configured count.
Observed performance control preserves stored control bits but substitutes the counter count, using the partition control when nesting below higher privilege and the configured count otherwise.

Performance enablement requires prior creation and validates interrupt configuration against controller mode, accepting only private or valid shared interrupts with an in-kernel controller and rejecting any configured interrupt without one.

First execution performs one-time preparation including topology compression, interrupt resource mapping, system state finalization, optional nesting allocations, trap computation, timer and performance enablement, private state finalization, and protected object creation before marking the VM as run.

Topology acceleration builds a compressed affinity to index table only for multi-CPU VMs, derives significance from bits differing across CPUs, bounds the table to a single page with fallback on overflow or allocation failure, and publishes for lock-free readers.

Nested control caching allocates a translation cache object only with a specific nesting feature, installs it once under the memory management lock with release visibility, and reports allocation failure if the cache remains absent.

Protected VM and CPU creation are idempotent guarded operations allocating page-granularity hypervisor memory, donating it through hypervisor calls, accounting pagetable pages, and recording creation; root sizing derives from address width and starting level controls.

Multiprocessing mutation serializes on a per-CPU state lock; pending scans nest an active-list lock outside per-interrupt locks with interrupt state preserved; private updates use scoped per-interrupt guards; topology and protected creation use a configuration lock with slot lock ordered outside it; cache install uses a write lock.

Observed CPU interface state includes per-group active priority arrays and a used count for older hardware, and enable plus mask control, running priority bitmap, packed private priority registers, and residency flag for newer hardware; common view carries enable, mask, grouping, acknowledge, and binary point fields.

Topology data carries an affinity significance mask plus a compressed identifier to vCPU index array; protected state carries creation flags, hypervisor handles, and memory caches; residency and run-once progress are tracked with flags and a per-CPU active identifier that can be invalidated.

Interrupt element residency moves between resident and nonresident with doorbell choice on release and refresh only on wait exit; VM execution moves from never-run to has-run once with finalization flags preventing repeat creation; initialization and finalization gate first run.

Invalid active-register selectors, unknown distributor models, and physical queries on non-hardware interrupts are programming errors; host queries warn on failure; repeated release without a residency guard would lose control state; oversized topology tables fall back rather than over-allocate.

Runnable, stopped, and suspended states, sleep and suspend requests, invalid-argument and memory and permission failure codes, private iteration bound, and narrow priority field placement in packed registers form the stable contracts observed here.
Clearing the active virtual machine identifier writes an invalid marker into the current CPU slot so later lookups do not reuse a stale identifier.
Finalization check passes unconditionally except for vector-capable CPUs, where it additionally requires vector state finalization.
